newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices fall as Iran issue seen easing.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall as Iran issue seen easing.

text.p: World oil prices slipped slightly on Tuesday, partly on positive market sentiment that Iran was trying to solve its latest crises with the European Union.

The May futures contract for world benchmark crude Brent Blend was trading 19 cents a barrel down at $18.00 a barrel at 1705 GMT on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), after hitting a low of $17.87 earlier in the day.
Brokers said there was positive sentiment in the market that there would not be an escalation in the dispute between Iran, the world's third largest crude exporter, and the European Union.

Crude oil prices moved up on Monday partly on a weekend report in the Washington Post, attributed to U.S. and Arab officials, linking a top Iranian government official to a group suspected of the 1996 bombing of a U.S. military compound in Saudi Arabia.
That report came hard on the heels of a German court's ruling on Friday that Iranian leaders were behind the killing of Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.
But oil brokers said they did not expect the European Union to mimic Washington's blanket ban on trade with Tehran.
"The Iran issue has to escalate a lot further before we start to see the oil markets paying too much relevance," one IPE trader said.
"As we know, a co-ordinated European action against Iran is not going to be something that will be easily pulled off. It's going to take a lot of bureaucracy," the broker said.
"I get the impression that the Iranian situation is already being pushed to the side (in oil markets)," he added.
The market was focusing instead on predictions for weekly U.S. stocks data. The American Petroleum Institute (API) is due to publish figures after the market closes on Tuesday.
Some traders were optimistic that the recent sharp drop in oil prices due to supply outweighing demand could be reversed.

Kuwait's oil minister, Isa al-Mazeedi, told a London-based newspaper in an interview that he believed the current glut would continue into the second quarter of the year but higher demand for gasoline should keep prices steady.

"All indications are that the current production glut will continue in the second quarter of the year but because this period sees demand rising for light products...and the industry begins to build stocks, these factors should minimise the impact on prices," Mazeedi told Asharq al-Awsat newspaper.
"You have to look at the United States as a big sponge that can absorb a lot of crude...and the overhang that we saw for the last two weeks can easily be absorbed," the trader said.
